paras: The killing of James Offutt was the fatal shooting of James Offutt, a Black man serving as a special policeman at a baseball game, by Lee Cozart, deputy marshal of Earlington, Kentucky, on the evening of August 19, 1900. Cozart was prosecuted by the Commonwealth and, after an examining trial before County Judge John G. B. Hall at Madisonville, was discharged. The Earlington Bee covered the case at length because both men were well regarded locally, and it printed the judge's full opinion.

On Sunday, August 19, colored baseball teams from Earlington and Madisonville played on the ball grounds near the lake at Earlington, in Hopkins County. Offutt had been sworn in as a special policeman for the day to keep the peace on the grounds, although Judge Hall later found that he had not been lawfully appointed and was not in fact an officer. The Bee described Offutt as "one of the first men of his race in Hopkins county" and Cozart as a quiet, industrious business man who had often served as deputy marshal.

After the game, Offutt disarmed a Madisonville man named Perry who had been flourishing a revolver, and he was holding a pistol in an excited crowd when Cozart drove up in his buggy. According to the Bee, Cozart remarked "there is a man with a gun" and went toward Offutt with his billy and pistol drawn. In the struggle that followed, Cozart struck Offutt over the head with the billy and then shot him under the chin, the bullet ranging upward and causing instant death. The shooting took place at about 6:30 p.m.

That night the nearest magistrate, acting as coroner, held an inquest whose jury found that Offutt had been shot in the head by Lee Cozart. The examining trial took a full day, and a large number of witnesses testified for both sides. Judge James Breathitt of Hopkinsville conducted the Commonwealth's case and argued for holding Cozart on a charge of manslaughter, while Jerrold Jonson and C. J. Waddill spoke for the defense.

Judge Hall ruled that each man had believed he was doing his duty as an officer, but that from Cozart's standpoint he had been arresting a man who resisted, and he discharged him. Hall called it "an unfortunate affair, but one for which the defendant can not be blaimed," and said there was no reason for ill will between the colored men of Earlington and Madisonville or between white and colored citizens. No report of a grand jury or further proceedings appears in the coverage.

The Bee, Earlington's own weekly, called the killing a "deplorable tragedy," said it counted both men among its friends, and declined to print the inquest testimony until all the evidence had been heard. A week later it printed Judge Hall's opinion in full under the headline "MAKES IT ALL A FEARFUL MISTAKE."

Papers farther away gave the case a line or two. The Hopkinsville Kentuckian, in its local column on August 24, presented the officer's version as fact: "The negro was trying to shoot the officer." On August 30 the Louisville Courier-Journal's "Kentucky News in Brief" reported only that Cozart had killed "James Offut, colored, at a negro baseball game" and had been released after his examining trial. No Black-press report of the killing appears in the coverage.

As the Bee summarized the evidence, the prosecution held that Cozart was hasty and that Offutt tried to ward off his blows and asked for time to explain, while the defense held that Cozart did not know Offutt was an officer and fired because Offutt resisted and presented a pistol. Judge Hall found that Offutt reached toward his vest and then held his pistol up "as if trying to strike or shoot," and that Cozart struck him at least twice, though some witnesses said four or five times. Cozart swore he saw no police star on Offutt, but a Commonwealth witness testified that he picked the star up from the ground and pinned it on Offutt after he had been killed.

reader.title: Killing of James Offutt
bases: A deputy town marshal shot and killed a Black man while trying to arrest him; no mob or crowd took part in the killing (A1, A2, A4).

Three papers (the local Bee in three items, the Hopkinsville Kentuckian, and the Louisville Courier-Journal) agree that Deputy Marshal Lee Cozart shot and killed James Offutt at Earlington, and an inquest verdict names Cozart (A1, A2, A3, A5); what led to the shot is disputed (A2, A4).

accounts.label: Prosecution (as summarized by the Bee)
accounts.gist: Cozart was hasty and the shooting unwarranted; Offutt tried to ward off Cozart's blows and asked for time to explain.

accounts.label: Defense (as summarized by the Bee)
accounts.gist: Cozart did not know Offutt was acting as an officer or who he was; Offutt resisted arrest and presented a pistol, so Cozart feared for his life and fired.

accounts.label: Judge Hall's findings
accounts.gist: Each man thought he was doing his duty; Offutt raised his hand toward his vest as if to draw, Cozart struck him, and Offutt had his pistol out and up as if to strike or shoot; seen from Cozart's standpoint it was resistance to arrest and Cozart was not to blame.

accounts.label: Hopkinsville Kentuckian item
accounts.gist: States flatly that 'the negro was trying to shoot the officer'.

framing.detail: The Earlington Bee called the killing a 'deplorable tragedy', counted both men among its friends, praised Offutt's character, laid out both sides, and later headlined the judge's opinion 'MAKES IT ALL A FEARFUL MISTAKE'.
The Hopkinsville Kentuckian's one-line item gave the officer's version as fact: 'The negro was trying to shoot the officer.'
The Courier-Journal reported only that Cozart had killed 'James Offut, colored, at a negro baseball game' and was released after an examining trial.

conflicts.field: whether Offutt threatened Cozart with a pistol

versions.value: Offutt tried to ward off Cozart's blows and asked for time to explain; the shooting was hasty and unwarranted (prosecution)
Offutt resisted arrest and presented a pistol at Cozart (defense); he was trying to shoot the officer (Kentuckian)
Offutt reached toward his vest and then had his pistol out and up 'as if trying to strike or shoot' (judge's finding)

conflicts.note: Every version is filtered through white papers; the Kentuckian's statement matches the defense claim. The judge's finding is the most detailed and was made after hearing many witnesses, but it is one side's reading of contested testimony.

conflicts.field: whether Cozart knew Offutt was acting as an officer

versions.value: Cozart swore he did not know; the defense said he did not know the man was Offutt
A police star had been on Offutt that afternoon; a witness said he picked it up from the ground and pinned it on Offutt after his death; Offutt called Cozart by the regular officer's name

conflicts.note: The judge took both points into account and accepted that Cozart did not know.
